query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (HEA) that is initially single phase, controlled thermal treatments that promote fine-scale phase decomposition—leading to the formation of incoherent precipitates preferentially along grain boundaries—cause a transition from ductile to brittle behavior. This mechanism is distinct from conventional alloys where brittleness predominantly arises from grain-boundary segregation or the formation of large, brittle intermetallic phases.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., an AlCoFeNi-based system) with a uniform microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled annealing treatments at temperatures that are low enough to slow diffusion and promote nanoscale phase separation, thereby inducing fine-scale decomposition into a mixture of ordered and disordered phases.
generation.conditions: Samples are subjected to the annealing treatment followed by mechanical loading (e.g., tensile or fracture toughness testing) at both room and elevated temperatures. A controlled comparison is made with a baseline sample retained in the as-cast single-phase state.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanometer- to sub-micrometer-scale incoherent precipitates forming along grain boundaries resulting from the phase decomposition (e.g., a mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC phases).
generation.mechanism: The formation and localization of these fine precipitates at grain boundaries lead to stress concentration and lowered grain-boundary cohesion during mechanical loading. This mechanism promotes crack initiation and propagation, ultimately causing brittle failure, in contrast to conventional behavior that is linked mainly to element segregation or coarse intermetallic grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast, single-phase baseline, the annealed HEA is expected to exhibit a measurable reduction in fracture toughness and increased brittleness due to the grain-boundary precipitation and associated microstructural inhomogeneity.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or solution-treated single-phase HEA with a uniformly ductile microstructure and high toughness.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is valid under thermal treatments that induce nanoscale phase decomposition without significantly altering the alloy’s overall composition. Service conditions include environments where the alloy is exposed to moderate thermal excursions and standard mechanical loading rates; extreme conditions (e.g., very high strain rates or temperatures far outside the treatment range) are not covered.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical precipitate size and volume fraction responsible for the brittle transition are uncertain and may vary with alloy composition. Additionally, the role of additional environmental factors (e.g., magnetic effects in related systems) remains to be fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one retained in the as-cast, single-phase condition and the other subjected to controlled annealing designed to induce nanoscale phase separation. Use advanced microscopy (e.g., TEM, high-resolution SEM) to characterize precipitate size, distribution, and localization, particularly at grain boundaries. Conduct standardized fracture toughness and tensile tests at relevant temperatures to compare the mechanical performance of both sample sets.
measurements: Quantitative microstructural analysis to determine precipitate volume fraction, size distribution, and location.
Fracture toughness (K_IC) and tensile ductility measurements to quantify brittleness.
Correlation analysis between the extent of grain-boundary precipitate formation and mechanical performance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a significant decrease in fracture toughness (or otherwise indicate brittle behavior) correlated with the presence of nanoprecipitates at the grain boundaries relative to the baseline single-phase samples, then the hypothesis that such phase decomposition drives brittleness in these HEAs will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.
We developed high-temperature high-damping high-entropy alloys with superior mechanical properties via Snoek relaxation.

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution.
